400.title: The path, closed
400.hook: eight factors, walked together, not one after another
400.howItsDone: Buddhists across schools teach the eight factors as three trainings, virtue, concentration and wisdom, developed together rather than in sequence; the eight-spoked wheel is widely used as a symbol of the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fourth jhana, and your line, wrapped in white. Did you meet one pleasant and one unpleasant moment with the same even attention? Day four hundred.

A wheel with eight spokes. It's painted on temple roofs, printed on flags, carved into stone. No spoke turns first. No spoke waits its turn. Pull one out and the whole wheel wobbles; it turns together or not at all. For forty-eight days we've walked the eightfold path one factor at a time, because that's how you learn a list. But it isn't how the path is walked. Today: the path, closed.
screen: `EIGHT SPOKES, ONE WHEEL.` → `NO SPOKE TURNS FIRST.` → `FORTY-EIGHT DAYS, ONE PATH.`

segments.voice: Here are the eight once more: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. In MN 44, a nun named Dhammadinna is asked about the path by a layman, Visakha, and she sorts the eight into three trainings. Speech, action and livelihood belong to virtue. Effort, mindfulness and concentration belong to concentration. View and intention belong to wisdom. The Buddha, told of her answers, says he would have answered the same way. Then MN 117 shows how the eight run into each other. Right view comes first, the Buddha says: knowing wrong speech as wrong and right speech as right, wrong action as wrong and right action as right. Right effort works to make the change. Right mindfulness remembers to. Those three, view, effort and mindfulness, run around each of the other factors, like friends walking alongside. So nobody finishes right view before starting right speech. You speak a little more carefully, and your view clears a little. Your view clears, and your work changes. Your work changes, and the mind gathers more easily. The Dhammapada says it in one line, in Max Müller's translation: “The best of ways is the eightfold.” The Pali word for path, magga, is an ordinary word for a road you walk on. And a road isn't walked one foot at a time, first all the left steps, then all the right. Both feet, the whole way.
screen: `VIRTUE, CONCENTRATION, WISDOM.` · `RIGHT VIEW GOES FIRST.` · `VIEW, EFFORT, MINDFULNESS RUN AROUND ALL.` · `THE BEST OF WAYS IS THE EIGHTFOLD.` · then, large: `EIGHT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the eight pass through, one breath each. First breath: view, seeing things as they are. Second: intention, goodwill. Third: speech, the words you'll use today. Fourth: action, harming no one. Fifth: livelihood, your work. Sixth: effort, the good you'll keep going. Seventh: mindfulness, this breath. Eighth: concentration, gathered here. Then let go of the list, and sit with all eight at once, nothing left out. The bell holds the time.
The path. Eight factors, walked together like the spokes of one wheel, each one strengthening the rest.
Your line: eight together. Today, pick one ordinary task and count how many of the eight are already in it. Day four hundred.

match.prompt: match each training to its factors.
pairs: the nun who sorted the eight

myth: the eight factors are mastered strictly in order, one by one
they're walked together; each strengthens the others.
in MN 117, right view, effort and mindfulness run around every other factor
view sees, effort changes, mindfulness remembers.

Dhammadinna, and the Buddha says he'd have answered the same.

fork.setup: in MN 117, the Buddha says one factor leads the way for the others. which one?
fork.reveal: right view comes first: knowing wrong as wrong and right as right. then effort and mindfulness walk with it around every other factor.

original.note: Pali ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo: the noble eightfold path; aṅga means a limb or factor, not a step.

trapdoor: what you thought: eight steps, climbed one after another.
what it means: eight factors developed together, each supporting the rest.
what a scholar hears: aṅga means a limb, a factor, not a rung; MN 117 calls right view the forerunner, and MN 44 groups the eight into the three trainings of sīla, samādhi and paññā.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 44, Culavedalla Sutta (Dhammadinna and the three trainings)
Majjhima Nikaya 117, Mahacattarisaka Sutta (right view comes first)

401.title: The Middle-Length Sayings
401.hook: 152 discourses of middle length; we read highlights in order, with Chalmers' translation
401.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Majjhima Nikaya is studied in monasteries and recited in Pali, and many lay Buddhists read it in translation; its suttas are often the texts teachers return to for instruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the path, and your line, eight together. How many of the eight did you find in one ordinary task? Day four hundred one, and a new block begins.

Some books you read cover to cover. Some you live in. For the next hundred and twenty-one days, we're going to live in one: the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle-Length Sayings of the Buddha. Not every page, but its highlights, in order. Here's some of what's coming. A man who sits alone in a forest at night until fear arrives. A raft. A saw. A water snake. A murderer who becomes a monk. A man shot with a poisoned arrow who won't let the doctor touch it until he knows who fired it. Today: the book itself.
screen: `A BOOK TO LIVE IN.` → `A RAFT, A SAW, A WATER SNAKE.` → `THE POISONED ARROW.`

segments.voice: Nikaya means a collection, a group. Majjhima means middle. The discourse basket of the Pali canon holds five nikayas, sorted partly by length: the Long Discourses, the Middle-Length, the Connected, the Numbered, and a collection of shorter books. The middle one holds a hundred and fifty-two discourses, longer than a page and shorter than a chapter, arranged in three sets of fifty, with fifty-two in the last. Who's speaking? Mostly the Buddha, but not only. Sariputta teaches. Mahakaccana unpacks a riddle. The nun Dhammadinna answers hard questions. Kings, brahmins, Jain ascetics and wandering philosophers all walk through, and a murderer named Angulimala. Many of the best-known teachings live here: the foundations of mindfulness in MN 10, the raft in MN 22, the noble search in MN 26, the poisoned arrow in MN 63, Angulimala in MN 86. Tradition says these discourses were recited together after the Buddha's death and carried for centuries by memory, by monks who specialized in chanting particular collections, before being written down in Sri Lanka around the first century BCE. In English, a translation by Lord Chalmers, Further Dialogues of the Buddha, appeared in the 1920s; we'll lean on it and on the Pali, mostly in our own retelling. One more thing you'll notice. This book has the feel of a real world. People argue. People misunderstand. Some walk away unconvinced. Not every discourse ends with everyone nodding, and the reciters kept those too.
screen: `NIKAYA — A COLLECTION.` · `152 DISCOURSES, THREE FIFTIES.` · `SARIPUTTA, KINGS, A NUN, A MURDERER.` · `CARRIED BY MEMORY, WRITTEN LATER.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE LENGTH.`

segments.voice: If you have the list of titles nearby, in a book or on a page, read down it slowly. If not, take these: the root of all things. All the taints. Heirs in the teaching. Fear and dread. The simile of the cloth. The simile of the saw. The water snake. The anthill. Let one title catch you, and don't ask why. Then put the list down, rest with the breath, and let that one title sit beside you. The bell holds the time.
Majjhima Nikaya. The Middle-Length Sayings: a hundred and fifty-two discourses, our book for the next stretch of the path.
Your line: the middle length. Today, read one thing of middle length all the way through, a long article, a letter, a chapter, without skimming. Day four hundred one.

screen: `DAY 401 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ROOT OF ALL THINGS.`

402.title: The root of all things
402.hook: the untaught make everything "mine", even nibbana; the monks were not pleased (MN 1)
402.howItsDone: Theravada monastics and scholars often study the Mulapariyaya Sutta as a famously difficult text; many teachers use it to point to the habit of making experience into 'me' and 'mine'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Majjhima Nikaya, and your line, the middle length. Which title caught you, and did you read one thing all the way through? Day four hundred two.

Most of the discourses end the same way: the monks were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One's words. It's the canon's version of a standing ovation, again and again. The very first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings ends differently. The Buddha finishes speaking, and in the edition most translators follow, the text says plainly: the monks did not delight in what he said. First discourse. First page. Not pleased. Today: the root of all things.
screen: `MOST DISCOURSES END DELIGHTED.` → `THE FIRST ONE DOESN'T.` → `NOT PLEASED.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Mulapariyaya, MN 1. The Buddha walks through everything a person could think of: earth, water, fire, air; beings and gods; the seen, the heard, the sensed, the known; unity and diversity; the all; and, last of all, nibbana. For each, he describes how an untaught person meets it. They perceive earth as earth. Then they conceive: they make earth into me, or put themselves in earth, or set themselves apart from earth; they think, earth is mine; and they delight in it. Why? Because, the Buddha says, they haven't fully understood it. The Pali verb is mannati: to conceive, to construe, to build a story with a self in it. And the startling part is the end of the list. Even nibbana, the end of grasping, can be made into a possession, conceived and delighted in. Then he describes someone in training, who knows earth directly as earth and is learning not to conceive. And the fully awakened, who don't conceive at all. Why weren't the monks pleased? The discourse doesn't say. A later commentary tells a story: these monks had been learned brahmins, proud of their scholarship, and the teaching was aimed at that pride. The Dhammapada makes a similar move in a single verse, in Max Müller's translation: “These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,” with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth? Not pleased is a fair place to start a book. Being bothered by a teaching sometimes means it found something.
screen: `EARTH, GODS, THE ALL, EVEN NIBBANA.` · `MANNATI — BUILDING A SELF-STORY.` · `KNOWING EARTH AS EARTH.` · `NOT PLEASED, ON PAGE ONE.` · then, large: `NOT PLEASED, YET.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let things come: a sound, a feeling in the body, a thought. Watch for a small move that happens next: my knee, my plan, my noise, my problem. You don't have to stop it. Just notice the word mine arriving, a half second after the thing itself. Sound as sound. Then, mine. See if you can catch the gap between them. The bell holds the time.
The root of all things. How an untaught mind turns whatever it meets, even nibbana, into me and mine.
screen: `THE ROOT OF ALL THINGS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not pleased, yet. Today, when a teaching or an idea bothers you, don't throw it out; leave it on the table for a day. Day four hundred two.

it says plainly that they did not delight in what he said.
the list of things people conceive includes nibbana itself

it doesn't; a later commentary tells a story about proud, learned monks.

fork.setup: the Buddha finishes the first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. how do the monks respond?
options: they delight in his words, as usual
they do not delight in his words
fork.reveal: they didn't delight. it's one of very few discourses that ends that way, and it sits on page one.

original.note: Pali maññati: to conceive, to construe; the verb MN 1 repeats for each thing the untaught make into 'me' and 'mine'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of philosophical categories.
what it means: how the mind turns whatever it meets into me and mine, even the highest goal.
what a scholar hears: the commentary says the listeners had been brahmins proud of their learning; its ending, 'the monks did not delight', is almost unique in the Pali discourses.

403.title: All the taints
403.hook: seven ways to deal with the taints: seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, removing, developing (MN 2)
403.howItsDone: Theravada monastics reflect on the four requisites, robes, food, shelter and medicine, as MN 2 describes, often by reciting a short reflection before using them; the destruction of the taints is a traditional description of awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the root of all things, and your line, not pleased, yet. Did something bother you, and did you leave it on the table instead of throwing it out? Day four hundred three.
screen: `THE ROOT OF ALL THINGS — NOT PLEASED, YET.`

segments.voice: An old wooden boat has a slow leak. Water seeps in at the seams. You can bail all day, and still, by evening, your ankles are wet. One seam needs caulking. Another only leaks when you scrape the rocks, so you steer around them. A third you just live with, and bail. Different leaks, different fixes, and the mistake is using one fix for all of them. The Buddha had a word for what leaks in a mind, and seven ways to deal with it. Today: all the taints.
screen: `A BOAT WITH A SLOW LEAK.` → `DIFFERENT SEAMS, DIFFERENT FIXES.` → `SEVEN WAYS.`

segments.voice: The word is asava, from a root meaning to flow. Translators reach for taints, cankers, outflows, effluents. In MN 2, the Sabbasava, the Buddha names three: the taint of sense desire, the taint of being, the craving to exist and keep existing, and the taint of ignorance. Then, instead of one remedy, he gives seven. Some taints are abandoned by seeing: understanding clearly, which we'll open tomorrow. Some by restraining: guarding the eye and the ear. Some by using: food, clothing, shelter and medicine used for what they're for, not for show or intoxication. Some by enduring: cold and heat, hunger and thirst, hurtful words and pain, borne patiently. Some by avoiding: a wild elephant, a thorny path, a cliff edge, and, listed right alongside them, bad company. Some by removing: when a thought of greed, ill will or cruelty comes, not putting up with it, but dispelling it. And some by developing: the seven factors of awakening. What makes this so practical is that it refuses to use one tool for every job. You don't endure a charging elephant; you step out of its way. You can't avoid hunger forever; some of it you simply endure. You don't restrain your way out of confusion; you look more clearly. A lot of frustration comes from using a good method in the wrong place. Seven ways, like a ring of keys: the skill is knowing which door you're standing at.
screen: `ASAVA — WHAT FLOWS.` · `THREE TAINTS.` · `SEVEN WAYS, NOT ONE.` · `THE RIGHT KEY FOR THE DOOR.` · then, large: `SEVEN WAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one thing that drains you: a habit, a craving, an irritation that keeps coming back. Then hold it up to the seven ways, slowly, one per breath. Seeing. Restraining. Using. Enduring. Avoiding. Removing. Developing. One of them will feel like it fits. Don't plan a whole campaign. Just choose the way, and rest with the breath, holding that choice lightly. The bell holds the time.
Asava. The taints: what flows in the mind and keeps it bound. Sense desire, the craving to be, and ignorance.
Your line: seven ways. Today, use the one way you chose, once, on the thing that drains you. Day four hundred three.

pairs: food and clothing for what they're for
a wild elephant, a cliff edge

it gives seven, each for a different kind of leak.

fork.setup: a wild elephant is charging down the path toward you. which of the seven ways does MN 2 recommend?
fork.reveal: avoiding. some things you endure; a charging elephant you simply get out of the way of.

original.note: Pali āsava: taint, outflow; from a root meaning to flow.

trapdoor: what you thought: taints, like stains on a shirt.
what it means: what flows in the mind and keeps it bound: sense desire, the craving to be, ignorance.
what a scholar hears: āsava also names a fermented drink, which is why some early translators chose 'intoxicants'; the destruction of the āsavas is a standard phrase for awakening.

404.title: Wise attention
404.hook: don't ask "did I exist in the past"; ask "what is dukkha, what ends it" (MN 2)
404.howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist schools emphasize wise attention, yoniso manasikara, as the ground of practice; Theravada teachers often present the four noble truths as a way of looking at any experience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: asava, and your line, seven ways. Which way did you choose, and did you get to use it once? Day four hundred four.

Three in the morning, and the questions start. Who am I, really? What was I before all this? Will any of it matter? What if I've got everything wrong? You can turn those over for hours and get up more tired than you lay down. About twenty-five centuries ago, the Buddha listed nearly the same questions, almost one for one. And then he said something surprising about them. Today: wise attention.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `WHO AM I? WHAT WAS I?` → `TIRED BY SUNRISE.`

segments.voice: In MN 2, the first of the seven ways with the taints is seeing, and seeing depends on how you attend. The Buddha describes unwise attention first. A person wonders: Was I in the past? Was I not? What was I in the past? How was I? Will I be in the future? What will I be? And about now: Am I? Am I not? What am I? Where did this being come from, and where will it go? Then they settle on a view. I have a self. Or, I have no self. Or some other. And the Buddha calls all of these a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a fetter of views. Notice that even I have no self is on that list, as a view to get tangled in. Then wise attention. The Pali is yoniso manasikara. Manasikara is attention, literally making in the mind. Yoniso comes from yoni, a womb, a source: attention that goes back to where things come from. And here is what it attends to: this is dukkha; this is its arising; this is its ending; this is the way to its ending. The four noble truths, used as questions. He doesn't call the big questions forbidden or foolish. He says they loop. The useful question is one that changes something: where is the suffering in this, what's feeding it, what would ease it? And the text says attention like this cuts three fetters: the view of a fixed self, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals. Not a small result, for changing what you ask.
screen: `WAS I? AM I? WHAT AM I?` · `A THICKET OF VIEWS.` · `YONISO — BACK TO THE SOURCE.` · `WHAT IS DUKKHA? WHAT ENDS IT?` · then, large: `THE USEFUL QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sit, and find a question that's been circling lately. Why does this always happen to me? What's wrong with me? Hold it for a breath. Then try turning it into a question about right now. Where is the tension in this, in the body? What's feeding it? What would ease it, even a little? You don't need answers. Just notice how the new question feels different in the chest. The bell holds the time.
Wise attention. Yoniso manasikara: attention that goes back to the source, and asks what is suffering and what ends it.
Your line: the useful question. Today, when a looping question starts, swap it once for this: what would ease this, right now? Day four hundred four.

pairs: what is dukkha, what ends it

he says they lead into a thicket of views, not out of dukkha.
in MN 2, even 'I have no self' is listed among the views
it's one of the views unwise attention settles on.
wise attention cuts three fetters, the text says
the view of a fixed self, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals.

fork.setup: it's 3 a.m. and you're asking: what was I in the past? what does MN 2 suggest?

fork.reveal: MN 2 turns attention to the four truths: this is dukkha, its arising, its ending, the way. even 'I have no self' is listed as a view to get stuck in.

original.note: Pali yoniso manasikāra: wise attention, attention by way of the source.

trapdoor: what you thought: wise attention means paying close attention.
what it means: attention that goes back to the source and asks what suffering is and what ends it.
what a scholar hears: yoniso is an adverb from yoni, womb or origin; MN 2 lists six views, including both 'I have a self' and 'I have no self', as products of unwise attention.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (taints abandoned by seeing)

405.title: Heirs in dhamma
405.hook: be my heirs in the teaching, not in material things (MN 3)
405.howItsDone: Many Buddhists describe the teaching as the most valuable gift, and in many communities giving or sponsoring copies of the teachings, or teaching others, is counted as a gift of dhamma.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wise attention, and your line, the useful question. When a question started looping, did you swap it for what would ease this? Day four hundred five.

Families can fight over the strangest things after a funeral. Not only the house or the savings. The good china. A watch. A recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting. What we inherit says something about who we were to the person who left. The Buddha, very much alive, once told his monks exactly what he wanted them to inherit from him, and then told a story to show he meant it. Today: heirs in dhamma.
screen: `THE CHINA, THE WATCH, THE RECIPE CARD.` → `WHAT WILL YOU INHERIT?`

segments.voice: MN 3, the Dhammadayada. It opens with one line: monks, be my heirs in the teaching, not my heirs in material things. The word for material things is amisa: flesh, food, the things of the body, and sometimes bait. Then the Buddha makes it concrete. Suppose, he says, I've eaten and finished my meal, and some food is left over, about to be thrown away. Two monks arrive, hungry and weak. I tell them: here is leftover food; eat it if you want, otherwise I'll throw it out. The first monk thinks: the Teacher said be heirs in the teaching, not in material things, and this food is a material thing. So he goes without, and spends the night hungry and weak. The second monk eats, and spends the night comfortably. And the Buddha says the first monk is the one more to be honored. Why? He says it will lead, for a long time, to fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, ease in supporting oneself, and energy. It's an uncomfortable story, and honest readers feel that. The point isn't that food is bad; the Buddha ate every day. The point is what you reach for when something is offered, and what that habit hands down. Then the Buddha gets up and goes into his dwelling, and Sariputta takes over, teaching how disciples keep the teaching alive by loving seclusion. The Dhammapada puts the value plainly, in Max Müller's translation: “The gift of the law exceeds all gifts.”
screen: `HEIRS IN TEACHING, NOT THINGS.` · `AMISA — FOOD, FLESH, BAIT.` · `TWO HUNGRY MONKS, ONE MEAL.` · `THE GIFT OF THE LAW.` · then, large: `INHERIT THE TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one thing you're holding onto that is only material: a purchase you keep circling, a comfort you reach for out of habit. Imagine setting it down, just for today. Now pick up one teaching from the last weeks to carry instead: the post holds, your own ground, seven ways, the useful question. Hold that one for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Heirs in dhamma. The Buddha's wish that his followers inherit his teaching, not his material things.
Your line: inherit the teaching. Today, pass on one thing you've learned to someone, instead of something you've bought. Day four hundred five.

pairs: teaches after the Buddha goes in

the Buddha ate every day; the point is what you reach for and hand down.
the Buddha calls the monk who went hungry more to be honored
for the sake of fewness of wishes and contentment.
amisa can also mean bait
flesh, food, worldly things, and the lure on a hook.

fork.setup: you're a hungry, weak monk. the Buddha offers you food he's about to throw away. what does the first monk in MN 3 do?
options: goes without, remembering 'heirs in the teaching'
fork.reveal: he goes hungry that night, and the Buddha says he's the one more to be honored. the second monk, who ate, did nothing wrong; the story is about what each chose to carry forward.

original.note: Pali dhamma-dāyāda: heir in the dhamma, the teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule about not eating leftovers.
what it means: carry forward the teaching, not the comforts: few wishes and a contented mind.
what a scholar hears: dhamma and āmisa form a recurring pair; elsewhere the suttas speak of two kinds of gift, of things and of dhamma, and call the gift of dhamma foremost.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 2 (two kinds of gift, of things and of dhamma)

406.title: Fear and dread
406.hook: alone in the forest at night, he met fear in whatever posture it found him (MN 4)
406.carry: face it where it finds you
406.howItsDone: In Thai and other forest traditions, monks have long practiced in wild and frightening places, including charnel grounds, as a way of meeting fear directly; many teachers also stress keeping precepts as a ground of confidence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: heirs in dhamma, and your line, inherit the teaching. Did you pass one thing you've learned on to someone? Day four hundred six, the end of the week.

Night in an old Indian forest. No electric light anywhere, only the moon, if that. A man sits alone in a grove that people say is haunted. A twig snaps. Leaves rustle. Something moves in the dark. And his heart pounds: here it comes, the fear, the dread. We know this because he told it himself, years later. It's the Buddha, before his awakening, describing nights he chose on purpose. Today: fear and dread.
screen: `A HAUNTED GROVE AT NIGHT.` → `A TWIG SNAPS.` → `HERE IT COMES.`

segments.voice: MN 4, the Bhayabherava. A brahmin named Janussoni says to the Buddha: forest life must be hard for a monk; the mind of someone without concentration would be swept away. Yes, says the Buddha; I thought so too, before. Then he explains two things. First, conduct. People who go into the forest with harmful actions, speech or ways of living, with greed or ill will, he says, call up fear and dread for themselves. He looked at himself and found his conduct clean, and that gave him great confidence in the wilderness. Second, the fear came anyway. On the special nights of the moon's fortnight, he went to the frightening places: shrines in parks and woods, under great trees. A deer would come by. A peacock would knock down a twig. The wind would stir the leaves. And he'd think: this is it, the fear and dread are coming. So he made a resolve. Why do I keep waiting for fear? Why not subdue it in whatever posture it finds me? If it came while he was walking, he kept walking until it passed; he didn't stand or sit or lie down. If it came while he stood, he stood. If he was sitting, he stayed sitting. If he was lying down, he didn't get up. He didn't run to a better position first. Notice what he never says: that he wasn't afraid. He says he met it where it found him. And the week closes here: the path walked whole, the Middle-Length Sayings opened, the root of all things, the taints, wise attention, the heirs, and the forest at night.
screen: `CLEAN CONDUCT, LESS DREAD.` · `A DEER, A PEACOCK, THE WIND.` · `MEET FEAR IN ANY POSTURE.` · `HE NEVER SAYS HE WASN'T AFRAID.` · then, large: `FACE IT WHERE IT FINDS YOU.`

segments.voice: Choose a small fear, not the biggest one: an email you haven't opened, a conversation you've been avoiding. Bring it to mind, and notice where it lands in the body: the stomach, the throat, the hands. Then do what the text describes: stay in the posture it finds you in. Don't shift, don't get up, don't reach for your phone. Breathe with it until it changes, even a little. The bell holds the time.
Fear and dread. Bhaya bherava: the terror of lonely places, met by the Buddha in whatever posture it found him.
Your line: face it where it finds you. Today, when a small fear shows up, stay right where you are for three breaths before you move. Day four hundred six.

pairs: says forest life must be hard

myth: the Buddha says he never felt fear in the forest
fear and dread came; he met them where they found him.
he chose frightening places on purpose
shrines in parks and woods, on special nights of the fortnight.
he waited until he was sitting down before facing fear
walking, standing, sitting or lying, he stayed in that posture until it passed.

fork.setup: you're walking alone in a dark grove and fear arrives. what did the Buddha-to-be do, in MN 4?
options: sat down to meditate on it
kept walking until the fear was subdued
fork.reveal: he kept walking. he didn't stand, sit or lie down until he'd subdued it. no better position first.

original.note: Pali bhaya-bherava: fear and dread, the terror of wild places; the name of MN 4.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about bravery.
what it means: fear met without moving, in whatever posture it arrives, grounded in clean conduct.
what a scholar hears: bhaya is fear, bherava is the dread of fearsome places; the special nights were the fourteenth, fifteenth and eighth of the lunar fortnight.
